blocks.text: I hung up and looked at my attorney, Rebecca Lin. "The bridge is open," I said. "People are driving on it right now."

She didn't hesitate. She called the Texas Department of Transportation's emergency line and the FBI field office in Dallas, in that order. I sat beside her and read the forged contract aloud over speakerphone to an engineer at TxDOT: which inspections had been waived, which load tests had been skipped, which steel specifications had been "adjusted."

The bridge carried a four-lane highway over the Trinity River. It had opened six weeks earlier with a ribbon-cutting and a high school band. By four that afternoon, state troopers had closed it in both directions.

Inspectors went in that night with lights and ultrasonic equipment. They found that the company had used cheaper, lower-grade steel bolts in more than three hundred critical connections and skipped the welding inspections that would have caught cracked joints.
One engineer told the news later that, under heavy truck traffic, the bridge might have lasted a year. Maybe less.
Nobody was hurt. That is still the sentence I repeat to myself when I can't sleep.

The CEO's plan had been simple and ugly. For two years, he'd used my name and a forged signature to approve the cost-cutting, pocketing the difference between the grant budget and what the company actually spent. When he learned a state audit was coming, he wired me two point three million dollars from the grant account so that, when the investigators followed the money, it would lead to my bank account. The accountant who'd "approved everything" and then received millions. He thought I'd be too greedy or too frightened to return it.
The FBI arrested him nine days later at his lake house, along with the company's chief engineer and an inspector who had signed off without visiting the site.
All three were convicted of fraud and endangering public safety.
I returned every cent of the two point three million, through my attorney, with a signed statement and a timestamp. I didn't take the fifty thousand either.
The bridge was repaired properly with new steel and reopened eighteen months later. On the day it reopened, I drove across it. Slowly. I was the third car.

I don't work in construction anymore. I teach forensic accounting at a community college. On the first day of class, I show my students a photo of the bridge and a copy of my forged signature. Then I tell them that the most important thing an accountant ever does is pick up the phone.
